title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document centralizes SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review requirements, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is the single-reference for on-call engineers, product owners, and platform teams responsible for maintaining Redwood production inference services.

Goals
- Establish consistent SLO targets, measurement windows, and alerting thresholds across Redwood services.
- Define standard error budget policies and automated actions on breach.
- Provide capacity planning methodology for GPU-backed inference infrastructure and shared platform services.
- Document reliability initiatives and ownership model for continuous improvement.
- Standardize incident review (postmortem) expectations and outputs.
- Describe operational tooling (metrics, tracing, logs, runbook storage) and provide canonical runbooks for common Sev1/Sev2 scenarios.

1) SLOs and SLIs (summary)

| Service | SLI | Target | Measurement window | Error budget | Primary owner | Pager threshold |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| API Gateway (edge) | P99 request latency (server-side) | 250ms | 30d rolling | 0.5% latency breach | eng-platform | page on 30m sustained breach |
| Hosted Text Inference | Successful token generation rate | 99.95% | 30d rolling | 0.05% failure | eng-serving-runtime | page at 4h sustained below target |
| Dedicated GPU Pool | Throughput (tokens/s per GPU) vs baseline | >=95% of baseline | 7d rolling | 5% degradation | eng-infra | page at 4h sustained below 90% |
| Embeddings Service | Request success (2xx within timeout) | 99.9% | 30d rolling | 0.1% failure | eng-serving-runtime | page at 3h sustained errors |
| Control Plane (job scheduling) | Job scheduling latency (95th) | 5s | 30d rolling | 1% | eng-platform | page on functional regression |

SLI definitions (concrete)
- Request success: HTTP 2xx responses where server completes work within configured deadline (include server-side timeouts). Exclude traffic tagged as synthetic or test.
- Latency: server processing time recorded at ingress proxy; P99 computed per 1h buckets then rolled into the configured window.
- Throughput: token generation rate measured at worker process and aggregated per GPU across cluster; normalizing for model architecture, sequence length, and hardware variant.

Measurement and tooling
- Primary metrics stack: Prometheus for real-time, Thanos for long-term retention and recorded rules.
- Recording rules must expose stable SLI series: slo:api_p99_latency_seconds, slo:inference_success_ratio, slo:gpu_tokens_per_second.
- Dashboards: Grafana per-service SLO panels, error budget burn-down, and alert history.
- Verification: daily synthetic canaries and end-to-end load tests in staging mirrored to production SLIs to catch instrumentation gaps.

2) Error budget policy and automated actions

Standard error budget window: 30-day rolling unless otherwise specified.

When an error budget is being consumed or breached:
- Warning (50% of budget consumed): owners receive a non-pager Slack notification and a weekly review is scheduled if trend continues.
- Action (80% consumed): product and infra owners must open an error-budget mitigation ticket and commit to actions; post within 48h.
- Breach (100% consumed): escalation to on-call lead and the service owner; triggers the following automated steps:
  1) Reduce risk: automatic temporary throttling of experimental routes and routes with no recent traffic using router policy.
  2) Canary rollback: if a rollout is in progress, abort/rollback to previous stable model or runtime variant.
  3) Capacity burst: enable reserved burst capacity policy for Dedicated customers (if available) to relieve pressure.
- Post-breach requirement: full incident review (see Incident Review Standards) and action items tracked in reliability backlog.

3) Capacity planning methodology

Inputs and cadence
- Quarterly forecasts for baseline growth provided by Product and Sales; monthly operational forecasts from infra telemetry.
- Capacity planning cadence: monthly operational review, quarterly strategic review tied to business forecasts and major launches.

GPU capacity model
- Unit: tokens/s per GPU for representative model families (e.g., default open LLM family). Curves maintained per instance type (A100-80GB, H100-80GB, etc.).
- Headroom target: maintain 30% spare capacity for burst tolerance and failover for Hosted API. Dedicated pools for committed customers are sized to meet SLA with 10% spare.
- Batching and KV-cache effects: model throughput measured at realistic batching configuration; capacity model includes batching factor and cold-cache degradation.

Forecasting process
1) Collect baseline utilization: 7d and 30d percentiles for tokens/s, request rate, and active sessions.
2) Apply growth assumptions from product launches or historical trend (P95 growth rate over prior 3 months).
3) Translate request-level forecasts to GPU capacity via tokens/s per GPU curves and planned latency SLOs.
4) Produce a capacity plan: procurement recommendations, cluster resizing schedule, and autoscaler tuning changes.

Capacity runbook triggers
- Trigger scaling review when any of the following occur:
  - 7d sustained GPU utilization > 75% of headroom-adjusted capacity
  - 3x increase in request rate over baseline within 24h
  - Errors correlated with CPU/GPU saturation

4) Reliability initiatives and program

Structure
- Reliability initiatives are tracked in the SRE reliability backlog in Jira with owner, impact estimate, and target milestones.
- Initiative types: infra work (autoscaler improvements), runtime optimizations (kernel tuning, quantization profiles), product mitigations (rate limits, retry strategies), observability investments (new SLIs, tracing improvements).

Process
- Monthly reliability triage: review top error budget consumers, recurring incidents, and initiative progress.
- Quarterly reliability sprint: focused 2-week block to address high-impact items with measurable SLO improvements.
- Post-initiative measurement: define success criteria before work (e.g., reduce error rate by X% or increase baseline throughput by Y tokens/s) and measure for 30d post-deploy.

5) Incident review standards (postmortems)

Timeline and ownership
- Postmortem required for Sev1 and Sev2 incidents that impact SLOs or customer SLAs. Owner: incident commander (IC) within 48h.
- Draft postmortem published within 72h; final postmortem with action items and owners published within 7 days.

Minimum postmortem contents
- Title and incident severity
- Timeline of events (UTC) and detection mechanism
- Impact summary (customers affected, SLO impact, duration)
- Root cause analysis (avoid blamestorming; focus on causal chain)
- Contributing factors and systemic issues
- Actions: immediate mitigations, medium-term fixes, and long-term initiatives with owners and due dates
- Error budget impact and verification plan
- Lessons learned and follow-up meeting scheduled

Review
- Postmortems are reviewed in the Reliability Review board weekly. High-impact postmortems are presented in the monthly reliability meeting.

6) Operational tooling and observability

Core tooling
- Metrics: Prometheus + Thanos, recording rules for SLIs and service-level metrics.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry/Jaeger. All services must propagate trace context from edge to model workers and control plane.
- Logs: structured JSON logs shipped to Elasticsearch/Opensearch with 30-day hot retention and 365-day cold retention for compliance tiers.
- Alerting: Alertmanager with alert routing by service and urgency. Pager rules defined in PagerDuty with runbooks linked.
- Runbook storage: canonical runbooks live in Confluence under eng-sre and are referenced by pager alerts. Runbook revisions must include owner and last-updated.

SLO burn and alerting rules
- Burn rate alerts for proactive response: 6x burn over a 1h window triggers a warning; sustained 6x over 3h triggers pager.
- Operational alerts should target actionable symptoms (CPU/GPU throttling, queue depth, excessive retries) rather than abstract SLO breaches alone.

7) Canonical runbooks (examples)

Runbook: Model process OOM or GPU OOM
- Symptom: Elevated OOM errors in worker logs, GPU memory utilization >95%, failed requests with 5xx and OOM text.
- Immediate actions:
  1) Page on-call for inference runtime.
  2) Identify recent deploys or config changes: check last 2 deploys and quantization profile changes.
  3) If a rollout is in progress, rollback the rollout and mark as paused.
  4) If persistent, scale down batch size via dynamic config to reduce memory pressure.
  5) If degradation continues, divert traffic to compatible smaller model variant and enable burst capacity for Dedicated pools.
- Post-incident: open action item to reproduce in staging and add a regression test.

Runbook: Degraded throughput across GPU pool
- Symptom: GPU utilization high but tokens/s low, increased queue depth, longer latencies.
- Immediate actions:
  1) Check autoscaler state and event logs; ensure new nodes are joining successfully.
  2) Validate kernel/driver versions across fleet for drift.
  3) Temporarily reduce batching to prioritize latency if requesters are latency-sensitive.
  4) If autoscaler stuck, manually add capacity using the provisioning playbook and notify infra.

Runbook: Control plane scheduling failures
- Symptom: Jobs stuck in pending for >30s, scheduler errors in logs, control plane 5xxs.
- Immediate actions:
  1) Page control plane on-call and run the scheduler health checks.
  2) Restart scheduler process if degraded and observe for repeat.
  3) If caused by DB connectivity, failover to read replica following DB runbook.

Runbook: Cache miss storm (prefix/KV cache)
- Symptom: Spike in cold cache misses, sudden increase in latency and GPU work.
- Immediate actions:
  1) Identify scope: is traffic new customers, rollout, or synthetic test traffic?
  2) Backfill cache with common prefixes for popular routes if feasible.
  3) Temporarily limit new-request rate with token bucket per-API-key and prioritize warm traffic.

8) RACI, ownership, and on-call expectations

RACI highlights
- SLO definition: Product (R), SRE (A), Eng runtime (C), Legal/Compliance (I)
- Capacity planning: Eng-infra (R), SRE (C), Product (A)
- Incident management: On-call IC (R), SRE lead (A), Service owner (C)

On-call rules
- Primary on-call is expected to acknowledge pages within 5 minutes for Sev1 and 15 minutes for Sev2.
- Escalation: after 15 minutes for Sev1 the page escalates to on-call lead; after 60 minutes, exec on-call is notified.
- Post-incident: the on-call must ensure postmortem ownership and at least one follow-up action is assigned.

9) Documentation hygiene and review cadence
- Runbooks must be reviewed at least quarterly and after every Sev1 incident.
- SLOs must be reviewed semi-annually with Product and Sales for alignment with customer expectations and SLAs.
- Ownership metadata (owner_team, author, last_updated) must be present on each Confluence page.

Appendix: Templates and quick checks
- Postmortem template: title, timeline, impact, RCA, actions, owner, due date.
- Quick triage checklist for on-call: verify instrumentation, check recent deploys, confirm autoscaler health, narrow blast radius.
